title: Direct, Indirect, and the Rest
lede: The grill is not a hot box — it is a heat-control instrument with two zones. Master where to put the meat, when to pull it, and how long to rest it, and the barbecue hosts itself.

blocks.html: Every grilling disaster reduces to a single geometry problem: heat arrives at the surface far faster than it can conduct to the centre. Push the fire hard enough to brown the outside of a thick steak and you overshoot the core; back the fire off to protect the core and you get grey, flabby meat with no crust. Beginners treat this as a skill they lack. It is not — it is a control problem with a clean solution.

That solution is the two-zone fire: build one hot side for browning and one cool side for gentle cook-through, then move the food between them on your schedule rather than the fire's. It is the same move as pulling a shot and then diluting to taste — you separate the two variables (surface reaction and internal temperature) so you can dial each independently. Once you internalise that, "steak, burgers, ribs, chicken, kebabs, pork chops" stop being six recipes and become one instrument played six ways.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.html: Browning (the Maillard reaction) runs fast above ~150 °C / 300 °F at the surface. Cooking the interior is heat conduction through meat — slow, roughly 0.1 cm² per minute of thermal diffusivity. A single fire hot enough for the first is far too hot to control the second. Two zones let you run each reaction in its own place at its own pace.

sections.title: Mental model — the grill as two instruments

blocks.html: Picture the grill from above as two territories. Over the coals (or lit burners) is the direct zone: radiant + conductive heat, 230–320 °C / 450–600 °F at the grate, the searing station. Beside it, over no fuel, is the indirect zone: with the lid down it becomes a convection oven at 120–180 °C / 250–350 °F, the gentle cook-through station. Food is not "on the grill" — it is in one of two rooms, and your whole job is deciding which room and for how long.

blocks.html: The single most useful consequence: the indirect side is a safe harbour. Flare-up? Move to indirect. Cooking too fast? Move to indirect. Guests not ready? Hold at indirect. You are never trapped by the fire because there is always a cooler room to retreat to. Coffee analogy: it is the bypass valve — a place to divert flow when the shot is running too fast.
Two routes to the same target

Given two zones, there are two orderings. Sear-then-finish: brown on direct first, move to indirect to coast up to temperature. Reverse sear: cook slowly on indirect almost all the way, then finish with a short blast on direct. For anything thicker than about 3 cm / 1¼ in, reverse sear wins, and the temperature trace shows why.

items.title: Maillard on live fire
items.html: What: the browning cascade of amino acids + sugars that builds crust, colour, and hundreds of aroma compounds, above ~150 °C / 300 °F. Why it matters: it is the entire reason to grill rather than boil — flavour lives on the surface. Common mistake: a wet surface. Water must boil off before the surface can climb past 100 °C / 212 °F, so a damp steak steams while it wastes fuel. Pat bone-dry, oil the food, and let a crust form before you touch it.

items.title: Doneness = internal temperature
items.html: What: texture and juiciness are set by peak core temperature, not by time or colour. Why it matters: it makes doneness a measured number, not a guess — an instant-read probe is your scale. Common mistake: cutting to peek (you release juice) or trusting the thumb-poke. Rare ~52 °C / 125 °F, medium-rare ~54–57 °C / 130–135 °F, medium ~60 °C / 140 °F. Probe the thickest point, away from bone.

items.title: Carryover cook
items.html: What: after you pull the meat, heat stored in the outer layers keeps conducting inward; the core coasts up another 3–5 °C / 5–9 °F (more in big roasts, up to 6–8 °C). Why it matters: if you pull at target you overshoot. Common mistake: ignoring it. Pull ~3 °C / 5 °F below target for steaks, more for roasts, and let the rest finish the job.

items.title: Ground meat is different
items.html: What: grinding takes surface bacteria — which on a whole steak stay on the outside where the sear kills them — and folds them throughout the patty. Why it matters: the interior is now the risky part, so it must reach a safer temperature. Common mistake: a "medium-rare" burger from shop-ground beef. Cook to ~71 °C / 160 °F unless you grind fresh from seared-then-cooled whole muscle yourself.

items.title: Resting = juice retention
items.html: What: heat makes muscle fibres contract and squeeze fluid toward the centre and out; resting lets them relax and reabsorb it. Why it matters: the difference between juice in the meat and a puddle on the board is a few minutes of patience. Common mistake: slicing hot. Rest a steak 5–10 min, a roast 15–30 min, tented loosely so the crust doesn't steam soft.

items.title: Collagen → gelatin (low & slow)
items.html: What: tough cuts (ribs, shoulder, brisket) are full of connective-tissue collagen that only melts to silky gelatin when held ~70–90 °C / 160–195 °F for hours. Why it matters: you cannot rush it with higher heat — that just dries the muscle. Common mistake: pulling ribs at "steak" temperature and finding them chewy. They need time at low temp, not more heat.

blocks.label: Variable that matters most
blocks.html: Thickness. Below ~2.5 cm / 1 in, the interior heats almost as fast as the surface browns, so a single hot direct zone is fine (burgers, thin steaks, kebabs). Above ~3 cm / 1¼ in, the surface-to-core gradient dominates and you need two zones. Measure the cut, not the recipe.

blocks.label: What beginners get wrong about marinades
blocks.html: Acid, salt, and enzymes penetrate only a few millimetres in hours — a marinade mostly seasons and flavours the surface, it does not tenderise the core. Worse, excess acid (citrus, vinegar) denatures surface proteins and turns the outer layer mushy and pale — the ceviche effect. Salt is the exception: given time it diffuses deeper. For big cuts, a dry brine (salt 1–24 h ahead, uncovered in the fridge) beats a wet marinade for both seasoning depth and crust.
You need less than the shops want you to buy. The instrument that actually changes your results is a thermometer, because it turns doneness from folklore into a reading.

blocks.title: Kit — necessary / optional / waste of money

rows.value: Necessary. Fast (2–3 s) thermocouple or thermistor. The single highest-leverage tool in this module. ~£15–100.
Necessary (charcoal). Lights coals evenly in ~15 min, no lighter fluid, no petrochemical taint. Replaces fire-starting guesswork.
Necessary. Control without stabbing (stabbing vents juice). A wide spatula for burgers/fish.
Necessary-ish. A lid and adjustable top+bottom vents give you a real oven and airflow control. This is the platform.
Optional, excellent. Tracks pit + core over hours for ribs/roasts without opening the lid. Earns its keep once you cook low & slow.
Optional. Oak, hickory, fruitwoods for smoke flavour. A fist-sized chunk or two — not a bonfire.
Waste of money. Pressing burgers squeezes out the fat and juice you want. Sear marks are cosmetic; even browning beats stripes.
Avoid. Off-flavours and inconsistent lighting. A chimney is faster and cleaner.

blocks.label: Mediocre → Excellent
blocks.html: The tell of a competent griller is not the rig — it is that they probe. Guessing gets you 60 % right; a £20 thermometer gets you 95 %. Buy the boring tool before the exciting one.
This is the reference you will actually return to. Pull temperatures already subtract carryover — pull at the "pull" number and let the rest coast you to "final".

blocks.html: Once you can execute a reverse-sear steak, every other cook is a variation. Here is the full loop with the reasoning attached.

items.label: L1 — I get a sear and a safe interior
L3 — I tune zones, timing, smoke
L4 — I improvise across cuts & host

blocks.html:
1. Prep — dry brine. Salt the steak (about 1 % of its weight, ~1 tsp coarse per 450 g) 1–24 h ahead, uncovered on a rack in the fridge. Salt seasons deep and the airflow dries the surface — pre-loading both flavour and crust. Pat bone-dry before it goes on.
  2. Prep — build two zones. Bank lit coals to one side (or light half the gas burners). Confirm a hot direct side and an indirect side with the lid vents open. Target ~135 °C / 275 °F in the indirect chamber.
  3. Execute — coast on indirect. Steak on the cool side, lid down, probe in the thickest point. Let the core climb slowly to ~6–8 °C / ~12 °F below your target (e.g. ~46 °C / 115 °F for medium-rare). Slow rise = even interior + drying surface.
  4. Execute — rest the fire, dry the meat. Pull the steak, open the lid, let the direct side rip hot. A brief pause lets the surface dry further — dry surface browns faster and hotter.
  5. Execute — sear. Onto screaming direct heat, ~45–60 s per side, flipping when it releases cleanly (it tells you the crust has formed — don't force it). Optionally baste with butter/aromatics in the last 30 s. You want colour, not more interior cooking.
  6. Evaluate — probe. Instant-read the centre. Because you seared briefly and the interior was already near target, carryover is small (~2–3 °C). If you're a few degrees short, another 20 s on direct; if over, you've learned to pull earlier next time.
  7. Correction — rest. Board or rack, tented loosely, 5–8 min. Fibres relax and reabsorb juice; slicing before this dumps it on the board. Slice against the grain to shorten the fibres you chew.

blocks.label: Why reverse sear beats sear-first here
blocks.html: Searing a cold steak first drives a steep temperature gradient — the outer layer races ahead and forms a thick grey overcooked band before the centre catches up. Starting gently means the whole interior is already close to target and nearly uniform, so the final sear adds crust without adding a grey band. The dried surface also browns faster, so you spend less time searing and overcook even less.

fields.detail: One hot zone only; thick cut cooked entirely on direct heat. Surface hits browning temp long before the core warms.
Crust is dark/black but a probe reads cold in the centre.
Build two zones. For thick cuts, coast on indirect first (reverse sear) or move off direct the moment a crust forms and finish on indirect with the lid down. Probe, don't guess.

blocks.problem: Ribs came out tough and chewy

fields.detail: Cooked too hot and/or too short. Collagen never got the hours at 70–90 °C it needs to convert to gelatin; you dried the muscle instead of melting the connective tissue.
Meat is dry and rubbery; probe went in with resistance. If you pulled at ~74 °C thinking "cooked", that's the tell.
Low & slow: 105–120 °C / 225–250 °F for 4–6 h (spare ribs). Done is texture, ~90–96 °C / 195–205 °F, probe slides like butter. Wrap in foil partway to power through the stall.
Breast overshot 74 °C on direct heat; or thighs pulled too early so connective tissue stayed tight. Lean breast has almost no fat buffer.
Breast: stringy, pale, dry. Thigh: safe temp but chewy tendons.

Cook bone-in pieces mostly indirect, finish skin on direct. Pull breast right at 74 °C / 165 °F (or hold 60 °C to pasteurise juicier). Take thighs further, to 82–88 °C / 180–190 °F. Brine or dry-brine ahead.

blocks.problem: Meat sticks and tears on the grate

fields.detail: Flipped too early — the crust hadn't formed and released yet. Cold grate, wet surface, or unoiled food also glue proteins to metal.
It resists lifting and leaves skin/crust behind.
Preheat the grate hot, oil the food not just the bars, pat surfaces dry, and wait. A properly seared surface releases itself — when it lifts cleanly, it's ready to flip.
Rendered fat drips onto flame; the fire finds oxygen and flares. Fatty cuts + all-direct heat = grease fire.
Sudden flames, black sooty spots, acrid taste.
Move to the indirect safe harbour until it dies down — never squirt water (spreads grease). Keep a fat-heavy cook mostly indirect; trim excessive fat caps; lid down starves flare-ups of oxygen.

blocks.problem: Thick grey overcooked band under the crust

fields.detail: Steep thermal gradient from searing a cold cut hard on direct heat: the outer layers overcook while the centre catches up.
Cross-section shows a wide dull band between crust and the rosy centre.
Reverse sear. Bring the interior up gently on indirect first so it's near-uniform, then a short hot sear. Thin grey band, wide even centre.
Dirty white/grey billowing smoke from smouldering, oxygen-starved wood, or too much wood. Creosote deposits on the meat.
Harsh, ashtray-bitter finish; thick white smoke rather than faint blue.

Aim for thin blue smoke: clean combustion with enough airflow. Open vents (oxygen = fuel), use a modest amount of dry hardwood, and let the fire breathe. If it's billowing white, it needs more air, not more wood.

blocks.html: Change exactly one variable, hold the rest, and read the result off a probe or a knife cut. This is how the mechanisms stop being claims and become things you've seen.

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E1 — reverse sear vs sear-first

fields.detail: See the grey band form and the interior even out.
Two steaks from one piece, same thickness (≥3 cm), same salt, same grill, same final target 54 °C / 130 °F.
Steak A: sear hard on direct first, finish indirect. Steak B: coast on indirect, then brief sear.
B is rosy edge-to-edge with a thin crust; A shows a wider grey band under the crust.
Cut both in cross-section side by side. Photograph the gradient. Note which crust is darker for less searing time.

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E2 — rested vs cut immediately

fields.detail: Quantify juice retention from resting.
Two identical steaks cooked identically to the same temp, same board.
Steak A: slice immediately off the fire. Steak B: rest 8 min tented, then slice.
A leaves a visible puddle; B leaves noticeably less liquid on the board.
Cut on paper towels or a tared plate and compare the wet area / weigh the runoff. B should lose clearly less.

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E3 — marinade penetration, 30 min vs 8 h

fields.detail: See how shallow marinade penetration really is.
Same cut, same marinade (with visible colour — soy/paprika), same fridge.
Piece A marinated 30 min; piece B marinated 8 h.
Both show colour only a few mm deep; extra time barely deepens it (salt goes furthest).
Slice each in half and measure the coloured rim with a ruler. Note that flavour is a surface effect — this reframes what a marinade is for.

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E4 — burger safety logic (temp ladder)

fields.detail: Feel the texture change that safety costs in ground meat.
Same grind, same patty weight/thickness, same direct heat.
Pull three patties at 60, 66, and 71 °C / 140, 150, 160 °F.
Juicier at 60 but the interior is the un-seared, higher-risk part; 71 °C is the shop-ground safe target.
Note juiciness vs your risk tolerance, and why the same logic does not apply to a whole steak (surface bacteria, seared away).
A deep-brown crust and a safe, juicy interior, on demand.
Beginner
80/20 chuck patties ~2 cm, coarse salt, probe, two-zone fire.
Salt just before cooking; sear both sides on direct until a crust releases cleanly; move to indirect if flaring; probe to 71 °C / 160 °F; rest 2–3 min.
Even mahogany crust, no stuck bits, juicy but reads 71 °C.
Pressing with the spatula (squeezes out fat); flipping before release (tears); over/undershooting temp.
Salt only at the last second (early salt firms the texture); handle the meat as little as possible.

blocks.title: Reverse-sear steak to a called number

fields.detail: Hit a stated doneness (say medium-rare, 54 °C / 130 °F) three times running.
Intermediate
Thick steaks (3 cm+), dry brine ahead, probe, two-zone fire.
Coast on indirect to ~46 °C; rest fire hot; sear 45–60 s/side; probe; rest 6 min.
Cross-section rosy edge-to-edge, thin crust, final temp within 2 °C of the call.
Searing too long (grey band creeps back); forgetting carryover; wet surface = weak crust.
Log pull-temp vs final-temp each time; adjust your early-pull offset until it's dialled.

blocks.title: Hold a pit temperature for two hours

fields.detail: Keep an indirect chamber steady at 120 °C / 250 °F ± 10 °C using only vents.
Advanced
Kettle with vents, chimney of coals, leave-in pit probe, one wood chunk.
Light a modest fire; set bottom vent as the throttle, top vent mostly open; nudge in small increments and wait 10 min to see the effect before touching again.
Two hours within band; thin blue smoke, not white.
Over-correcting (oxygen = fuel, temp lags your changes); choking the fire into acrid smoke.
Treat the vent like a PID loop: small inputs, wait for the response, converge. Log vent position vs temp.

blocks.title: Burgers & kebabs with a real sear

fields.detail: Feed four with two-zone burgers and vegetable/chicken kebabs, everything crusted and cooked to temp.
Building two zones, direct searing, flare-up management, probing burgers to 71 °C.
Juicy burgers with even crust; kebabs charred outside, cooked through, not dried.
No raw centres, no charred-black outsides, no flare damage; you used the safe harbour at least once on purpose.

blocks.title: Reverse-sear steaks + grilled chicken, plated together

fields.detail: Run two cuts with different targets off one fire, resting timed so both land together.
Reverse sear, bone-in chicken indirect-then-direct, carryover budgeting, resting logistics.
Steak edge-to-edge medium-rare; chicken juicy at 74 °C breast / 85 °C thigh; both rested, none cold.
Every piece within 2–3 °C of its target; you sequenced the cook so nothing sat cooling.

blocks.title: Host a full barbecue: low-and-slow ribs for a crowd

fields.detail: Cook ribs (and/or pork shoulder) low & slow, plus quick-fire sides, and serve 6–8 guests on time.

Fire & vent control over hours, thin-blue-smoke management, riding the stall (wrap to push through), reading doneness by feel (probe like butter, ~93 °C / 200 °F), holding & resting while you finish direct-heat sides.
Tender, moist ribs with clean smoke flavour and bark; sides hot; guests fed within a 30-min window.
Meat pulls cleanly but doesn't fall to mush; no acrid smoke; you held pit temp without babysitting every minute; timeline worked backward from serving hour.

blocks.html: Train your eye on the things a thermometer can't tell you — smoke colour, crust, the fire's layout.

blocks.query: two zone charcoal grill setup coals banked
blocks.look: Look for: coals piled to one side, empty grate on the other. Note how much of the kettle is left as safe harbour.

blocks.query: thin blue smoke vs white smoke bbq
blocks.look: Look for: the barely-visible blue haze (good) versus thick billowing white/grey (acrid). This is the single best smoke tell.

blocks.query: reverse sear steak cross section grey band comparison
blocks.look: Look for: edge-to-edge pink of a reverse sear vs the wide dull band of a hard sear-first cook.

blocks.query: charcoal chimney starter lit coals ashed over
blocks.look: Look for: coals greyed with ash on top before dumping — that's "ready", not black-and-flaming.

blocks.query: pork ribs bend test bark done
blocks.look: Look for: the rack bending and cracking on the surface when lifted — a visual doneness cue alongside the probe.

questions: Why can you safely eat a rare steak but not a rare burger ground from the same piece of beef? What single number changes, and why?

A 4 cm steak comes off a hard direct-heat sear with a black crust and a
        cold centre. Explain the mechanism, and describe the two-zone fix and why it works.

Two identical steaks: one sliced immediately, one rested 8 minutes.
        Predict what the cutting board looks like under each, and explain the fibre mechanism.
Ribs pulled at 74 °C / 165 °F are tough; the same ribs held for hours to 94 °C / 200 °F are tender. Why does more heat, faster not fix the first batch?

You marinated a thick cut for 8 hours and the centre still tastes plain.
        Explain why, and say what you'd change to actually flavour/season deeper.

Your pit is billowing thick white smoke and the meat tastes bitter. Is the
        fix more wood or more air? Justify it in terms of combustion.

blocks.label: Answer key (mechanisms)
blocks.html: Q1 Surface bacteria on whole muscle stay outside where the sear kills them; grinding mixes them throughout, so the interior must reach ~71 °C / 160 °F. Q2 Surface browns far faster than heat conducts inward; two zones let you sear on direct then coast on indirect (or reverse-sear) to decouple crust from core. Q3 Sliced-hot leaves a puddle; rested reabsorbs — heat contracts fibres and squeezes juice out, resting relaxes them. Q4 Toughness is collagen, which only melts to gelatin over hours at 70–90 °C; higher heat just dries muscle. Q5 Marinades penetrate only a few mm; salt/dry-brine ahead diffuses deeper. Q6 More air — white billowing smoke is oxygen-starved smouldering; open the vents for clean thin-blue combustion.
Practical challenge

Run E1 (reverse sear vs sear-first) and E2 (rested vs immediate) on one cook, photograph both cross-sections and both cutting boards, and log your pull-temp vs final-temp. Then cook a rack of ribs low & slow, holding pit temp within ±10 °C for the duration, and take them to probe-tender by feel. Pass = even reverse-sear interior, visibly less board-juice on the rested steak, and tender (not mushy, not chewy) ribs with clean smoke.
Reflection

Where did you have to retreat to the safe harbour, and what was the fire telling you? Which reading surprised you most — the marinade penetration depth, the grey band, or the rested board? And having done it once: what would you change about your timeline to host eight people without the food ever sitting cold?
